title: The mountain goes home
hook: the smell of a mountain on the wind, an army rising, and a peak put back
carry: nishkama karma: do the work, don't claim the prize

segments.voice: Yesterday: the healing plants are alive, and holy. The plants hid, so Hanuman lifted the whole peak and flew it south like a second sun.

The monkeys still conscious see it first: a light in the northern sky, coming fast. Then they hear Hanuman's roar, and they roar back, weak and astonished. He sets down over the battlefield with a mountain in his hands, trees and rocks and all, glowing in the dark. And before anyone has picked a single leaf, something happens that nobody planned. The wind carries the scent of the herbs out over the field.
screen: `A LIGHT IN THE NORTH.` → `HANUMAN'S ROAR.` → `THE SCENT ON THE WIND.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki, that's all it takes. The smell of the herbs drifts over the fallen, and they rise. Rama and Lakshmana breathe in, the arrows come out of them, and their wounds close. All around them the monkeys and bears get up, shaking themselves as if they'd been asleep. Valmiki notes something about the other side, too. The rakshasas who had died didn't rise, because Ravana had ordered his dead thrown into the sea, so the enemy wouldn't see how many he'd lost. Then Hanuman does something the famous picture doesn't show. He picks up the mountain again, flies it all the way back north, sets it in its place in the Himalaya, and returns to the camp. He doesn't keep the prize or put it on display. The work is done, so the mountain goes home. Many teachers see in this the Bhagavad Gita's teaching of nishkama karma, action without craving its fruit: your right is to the work alone, never to its rewards. Devotees hold up Hanuman as the one who lives it. In the epic's last book, when Rama offers him a gift, Hanuman asks only that his love for Rama never fade, and that he live as long as Rama's story is told. In a later telling, the Ramcharitmanas of Tulsidas, Bharata shoots Hanuman down over Ayodhya as he passes. In Valmiki the trip is uninterrupted: north, south, north again, and back before the battle starts.
screen: `THE SCENT ALONE HEALS.` · `RAVANA HID HIS DEAD.` · `THE MOUNTAIN GOES HOME.` · `NISHKAMA KARMA.` · then, large: `DO THE WORK, DON'T CLAIM THE PRIZE.`

segments.voice: Breathe in slowly through the nose, as if something healing were on the air. Then bring to mind some good work you did lately that no one thanked you for. If you pray, offer it to God in your own words, the way the Gita asks: the work is mine, the fruit is yours. If you don't, breathe out the wish for credit, and keep the good of the work itself.
Mrtasanjivani, the herb that revives the dead. Its scent alone lifts the fallen army, and then Hanuman carries the peak home, keeping nothing for himself.
Your line: nishkama karma, do the work, don't claim the prize. Next, the same story as most people picture it. Rest well.

howItsDone: Hanuman's flight with the herb mountain is recited and sung in devotion to him, in Valmiki's telling and in later ones such as the Ramcharitmanas.
